Abdominal CT showed bilateral adrenal enlargement with a hyperdense central area (~2 cm, HU 25–35) in the right adrenal gland; no suspicious lesion otherwise.

Testing was negative for tuberculosis and multiple infectious causes (candida/aspergillus antigens, CMV DNA, HIV, treponema, and serologies for cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, trypanosomiasis). She was not taking medications known to interfere with adrenal function.

Treatment with oral cortisone acetate led to rapid symptom improvement and normalization of sodium; she was discharged on glucocorticoid replacement. Follow-up showed persistently absent cortisol response to ACTH stimulation for months, with very low DHEA-S and generally normal PRA/aldosterone later. Repeat CT at 6 months showed normalization of adrenal size and resolution of the prior right-sided hyperdense lesion; later imaging showed normal left adrenal and a smaller, inhomogeneous right adrenal. Over 30 months, basal cortisol and ACTH progressively normalized while continuing a minimal dose of cortisone acetate, but cortisol remained nonresponsive to ACTH stimulation.

case.diagnosis: Invasive papillary carcinoma of the breast
case.narrative: A breast papillary carcinoma subtype characterized by slow biological activity and gradual progression, typically luminal type, Nottingham grade 2, and low TNM stage. Compared with invasive ductal carcinoma, it shows more favorable pathology with lower tumor T stage, lower axillary lymph node metastasis rates (~11.6%–17.25% vs ~32.6%–50%), lower Ki-67, higher hormone receptor positivity, and lower HER2 amplification; larger tumor size and lymphovascular invasion are less prevalent. Reported case: 59-year-old with ~10-year natural history; large primary tumor (~10.4 × 7.2 × 3.5 cm) grew <2 cm over a decade without treatment, no distant metastases; IHC stable with ER/PR positive, HER2 (C-erbB2) negative, Ki-67 ~10%. Genomic features in papillary carcinoma subtypes show similarities (loss of 16q; gain of 16p and 1q), fewer aberrations and minimal p53 expression; PIK3CA mutations in ~40% have been observed; transcriptomic differences relate to cell adhesion/migration genes. Organoid drug sensitivity testing in a papillary carcinoma case showed high efficacy of fulvestrant among tested endocrine therapies.

Root-end resection (~3 mm) was performed with orthograde MTA obturation done prior to surgery; PRP and bone graft were placed, the cortical plate was repositioned and stabilized with PMMA-based bone cement, and the flap was sutured. Follow-up at 3 and 12 months showed the patient asymptomatic with radiographic evidence of complete healing.

Femoral reconstruction performed 15 weeks after injury: removal of implants, insertion of bipolar head prosthesis with long stem and proximal/distal interlocking screws; femoral shaft dynamization performed. Post-reconstruction: pain resolved; non-weight-bearing 4 weeks then gradual progression to full weight-bearing by 8 weeks. At 1 year: no activity restriction; radiographs with good callus formation in pelvis and femur and no prosthesis loosening.

Continuous NMP was performed for 110 minutes at 37°C with oxygenation; perfusion pressure 52–70 mmHg and flow 130–184 mL/min remained stable; perfusate creatinine and urea stayed low; the graft produced urine throughout and urine pH and specific gravity were comparable before procurement, during NMP, and after reperfusion. The graft was transplanted into the recipient right iliac fossa with re-establishment of an in vivo NMP circuit; donor suprarenal aorta and IVC were anastomosed end-to-side to the recipient right external iliac artery and vein using 6-0 Prolene; NMP was stopped after establishing recipient blood supply; approximately 50 mL perfusate was flushed; cannulas were removed and donor infrarenal aorta and IVC were closed; ureteroneocystostomy was performed. She had disorganized thoughts, poor sleep, rapid speech, labile mood, distractibility, auditory hallucinations, and grandiose delusions, and was placed on an involuntary psychiatric hold. She remained in the ED due to inability to place her on droplet precautions elsewhere and inability to reliably wear an infection-prevention mask. She had flu-like symptoms with a positive influenza swab and was started on oseltamivir. Over several days she had persistent agitation/aggression requiring multiple doses of antipsychotics/benzodiazepines (including haloperidol/lorazepam/diphenhydramine IM, olanzapine, chlorpromazine, clonazepam) and was started on valproic acid; she became increasingly somnolent with slurred speech, and on medical admission her valproic acid level was 166 mcg/ml. On the day she was medically cleared for psychiatric hospitalization, she developed difficulty breathing with hypoxia and tachycardia and bilateral expiratory wheezes; she was treated with bronchodilators. Chest X-ray suggested left-sided pneumonia and she received IV ceftriaxone, azithromycin, and fluids; CT angiography was obtained to evaluate for pulmonary embolism. She was admitted to medicine and then developed worsening agitation with respiratory distress and altered mental status, could not tolerate BiPAP, and was intubated for airway protection with hypoxic respiratory failure. CT angiography showed a sub-segmental pulmonary embolus; she was transferred to the MICU with combined hypercarbic and hypoxic respiratory failure attributed to COPD exacerbation with influenza, possible hospital-acquired pneumonia, and possible pulmonary embolism in the setting of prolonged ED stay/immobility, tachycardia, and high Well's score. She was started on heparin and improved, with resolution of respiratory distress and extubation the next day.

case.narrative: A 33-year-old woman developed a severe depressive episode 4 weeks after her first delivery, with sleep disturbance and guilt. No personal or family history of psychiatric disorders. Follow-up assessments every 2–4 weeks using the Quick Inventory of Depressive Symptomatology–Self Report (16 items). Marked symptom improvement by week 4 (notably sleep), remission by week 8. Biochemical tests for mother and infant remained normal; infant development normal; no adverse events reported during treatment or after discontinuation.

case.diagnosis: Acute Exacerbation of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
case.narrative: A 51-year-old female with self-reported bipolar disorder was brought to the emergency room by police for bizarre behavior at a bus stop with incessant yelling. She exhibited disorganized thoughts, poor sleep, rapid speech, labile mood, distractibility, auditory hallucinations, and grandiose delusions, and was placed on an involuntary psychiatric hold. She was treated with escalating doses of antipsychotics and benzodiazepines (including multiple IM emergency medication combinations) and later started on valproic acid for mood stabilization. She had flu-like symptoms with a positive influenza swab and was started on oseltamivir; she remained in the ED due to inability to place her in inpatient psychiatry with droplet precautions. Over subsequent days she became increasingly somnolent with slurred speech. On the day of planned psychiatric transfer, she developed dyspnea with hypoxia and tachycardia; exam showed bilateral expiratory wheezes and she was treated with nebulized bronchodilators. Chest X-ray suggested possible left-sided pneumonia; she received IV ceftriaxone and azithromycin and fluids, and CT angiography was performed. On admission to medicine, valproic acid level was 166 mcg/ml. She became increasingly agitated with respiratory distress, was altered and unable to tolerate BiPAP, and was intubated for airway protection due to mixed hypercarbic and hypoxic respiratory failure. CT angiography showed a sub-segmental pulmonary embolus; she was transferred to MICU, treated with heparin, and her respiratory distress resolved with subsequent extubation.

Evaluation for suspected airway foreign material included fiberoptic bronchoscopy showing a plant-like material in the right lower lobe bronchus with severely inflamed mucosa; removal attempt failed due to profuse bleeding. Chest X-ray and CT were obtained. Rigid bronchoscopy again found the material in the right lower lobe with extensive surrounding granulation tissue; removal attempts caused heavy bleeding and the object was fixed and could not be extracted. Thoracotomy revealed an inflammatory peripheral lung mass; opening the area entered a 2×2 cm pus-filled cavity containing the stalk, which was removed. The cavity was irrigated and a bronchial opening repaired; chest tube placed; postoperative broad-spectrum antibiotics given; chest tube removed after one week and discharged. Follow-up: mild hemoptysis with blood-streaked sputum during the first postoperative year; CT showed limited bronchiectasis localized to the affected area, which resolved with conservative management.

Labs: WBC ~10×10^9/L, hemoglobin 141 then 134 g/L, platelets normal; CRP <0.2 mg/L; normal coagulation; normal liver/biochem/myocardial enzymes/urinalysis/ESR; negative infectious testing (bacteria, mycoplasma, TB, fungi); normal echocardiogram. Chest CTA: intra-alveolar hemorrhage, partial right bronchial stenosis, right middle-lobe atelectasis, partial right lower-lobe consolidation; pulmonary CTA without significant abnormalities. CTA/angiography: bronchial arteries with abnormal origin/course and dilated lumen; aortic angiography showed an ectopic bronchial artery arising from the right renal artery supplying the right lower lung with tortuous/disordered peripheral vessels and early visualization of pulmonary artery branch suggesting a bronchial–pulmonary artery fistula. Interventional embolization performed (microspheres/coil) with cessation of hemoptysis. Post-procedure right lung atelectasis due to airway clot burden; bronchoscopy removed large clots from right main/upper/middle bronchi with resolution of symptoms and atelectasis. No recurrent hemoptysis during 1.5-year follow-up; chest radiographs normal.

case.narrative:
Age/Gender: 29-year-old male
Occupation: Professional surfer
Medical History: Generally healthy, active lifestyle, no previous major medical issues.
Presenting Complaint: Experienced a surfing accident two months ago, where he was thrown against a reef, striking his back. Initially had mild to moderate back pain, which has progressively worsened. Recently, he has noticed difficulty walking, increased clumsiness of hands, and occasional episodes of numbness and tingling in his extremities. The patient is increasingly concerned about the changes in his neurological function, particularly the impact on his professional and daily activities.
Vital Signs: Within normal limits. Physical Examination: Notable tenderness and mild swelling over the thoracic spine. Decreased range of motion due to pain.
Neurological Examination: Evidence of myelopathy, including hyperreflexia, positive Babinski sign, and a broad-based unsteady gait. Decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick in a glove-and-stocking distribution. Mild weakness in the lower extremities. X-rays of the Thoracic Spine: Confirm the presence of a compression fracture at T7 with some kyphotic deformity.MRI of the Thoracic Spine: Reveals a compression fracture of the T7 vertebra with retropulsion of bone fragments into the spinal canal, causing moderate to severe spinal cord compression. Evidence of spinal cord edema at the level of injury.
